short_definition: A growth mindset is the belief that abilities and intelligence can be developed through effort, good strategies and feedback, rather than being fixed traits you are born with.
explanation: The idea, popularised by psychologist Carol Dweck, contrasts a growth mindset with a fixed mindset. Someone with a growth mindset treats a hard task or a failure as information about what to practise next; someone with a fixed mindset tends to see it as proof of a permanent limit.

It matters because how you interpret setbacks shapes whether you keep going. With money and career skills — learning to budget, invest, negotiate or use new tools — beginners make mistakes, and a growth mindset helps turn those mistakes into lessons instead of reasons to quit.

The trade-off is that mindset alone isn't magic: effort without better strategies, feedback or resources can lead to frustration, and research on simple mindset interventions shows mixed effects. Use it as a lens alongside practical action, not as a replacement for it.
example: Illustrative example: After overspending by 150 in her first budgeting month, Lena thinks, 'I'm just bad with money' (fixed). She reframes it as 'My grocery category was set too low — I'll track it weekly next month' (growth), and the next month she overspends by only 40.
common_mistake: Equating a growth mindset with simply 'trying harder' or staying positive, instead of changing strategies and seeking feedback when something isn't working.
title: Growth Mindset
